item.title: A Senator Facing Re-Election Settles a Bakery Bill, 6 Years Later
item.description:
Senator Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, has faced a series of challenges in his unexpectedly close race for re-election.

The latest: A six-year-old unpaid bill for 150 frosted sugar cookies, 100 mini strawberry muffins and 100 fudge brownies, posted online by an angry baker.

The bill, the baker wrote in a social media post that quickly went viral on Thursday, was from Mr. Marshall’s primary night watch party in 2020. The cookies’ buttercream frosting carried his name in blue and yellow. And the source of her frustration was that Mr. Marshall’s 2020 campaign had never paid her the nearly $700 she said it owed her.

On Saturday, Mr. Marshall wrote on social media that he had paid the bill, bringing more attention to a curious saga that his opponent’s campaign had seized on.

The bill began gaining widespread notice on Thursday afternoon, after the baker, Holly Thomas of Hutchinson, Kan., wrote an eight-paragraph Facebook post.

“Six years later, I haven’t forgotten,” she wrote, recalling that repeated phone and email inquires seeking payment had gone unanswered. “That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote.”

Mr. Marshall, a first-term Republican who may need every vote he can get in a race that polls indicate is neck-and-neck, rushed to respond. He was already contending with a separate revelation about unpaid bills that he had sought to collect on: Last month, The New York Times reported that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, and that he had routinely charged patients an 18 percent annual interest rate.

On Thursday evening, Tyson Brody, a spokesman for the Rev. Adam Hamilton, Mr. Marshall’s Democratic opponent, amplified the baker’s post, writing on social media that the bakery bill was “larger than debts for which Roger Marshall had patients sued.” (The unpaid medical bills ranged from $101 to several thousand dollars.)

By Friday, Mr. Marshall had paid Ms. Thomas back, she said in an interview. On Saturday, he addressed the issue in a post on his official X account.

“As some folks may have seen, there was a post on social media regarding an unpaid 2020 cookie bill,” Mr. Marshall wrote. “We have absolutely no idea how this happened.”

But, he added, “as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double.”

The senator attached an invoice showing that he had sent $1,300 to Ms. Thomas’s bakery, Holly’s Sweet Treats. That amount was not quite double the original bill, which had been for $678.75, according to the copy that Ms. Thomas posted on Facebook this week.

It was not clear if Mr. Marshall’s response would satisfy some of the commenters who had seized on the initial post. One had argued that Mr. Marshall owed Ms. Thomas more than $1,400, accounting for interest.

Mr. Marshall’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for further comment on the bill. Several Republican strategists said that Mr. Marshall had handled an unfortunate situation as well as he could.

Ms. Thomas, for her part, said she still had no intention of voting for Mr. Marshall, though she added that his payment was “the right thing to do.”

“I can’t put all the blame on him,” said Ms. Thomas, 43, recalling that the initial order had been placed by a campaign staff member. “But as a business owner, when my staff messes up, it falls on me as well.”

She has been closely following the Senate race and “impulsively” wrote her post as she complained at work about the years-old order, she recalled.

“I just made a post about Roger Marshall and how he didn’t pay me,” Ms. Thomas said she had declared at work. “We’ll see what happens. Maybe he will pay me.”

By Thursday evening, her phone began pinging with messages as she watched her daughter’s volleyball game. She had a theory, she said, for why the post took off.

“He’s let a lot of people down in the state,” said Ms. Thomas, who declined to share her political affiliation. “And people are frustrated with how things are going.”

Some on social media accused Mr. Marshall of hypocrisy, citing his own business practices.

“I do think he’s a hypocrite,” Lindsey Derr, 43, a Democrat in Hutchinson, Kan., who had already planned to vote against Mr. Marshall, said in a phone conversation. She added, “It makes me very upset.”

Mr. Marshall is trying to avoid becoming the first Republican to lose a Senate race in Kansas since 1932. His campaign says the senator gets results for Kansas. But he has been challenged by steep price increases that the Iran war has inflicted on farmers in the state.

On Saturday, Mr. Hamilton’s campaign issued a statement that attempted to encapsulate the episode in a single word: “Cookiegate.”

Evan Gorelick contributed reporting.

item.title: America’s Elected Officials Are Living in Fear
item.description:
A Times investigation has found that violent threats have become a new normal among public officials, reshaped private lives, cost millions in security and pushed people out of office.

By The New York Times

A Times investigation has found that violent threats have become a new normal among public officials, reshaped private lives, cost millions in security and pushed people out of office.

Supported by

A Times investigation has found that violent threats have become a new normal among public officials, reshaped private lives, cost millions in security and pushed people out of office.

By Nick Corasaniti

Photographs by Haiyun Jiang

In January, a caller began leaving threats in the voice mail inboxes of members of Congress: “I want to see their throat cut from ear to ear.”

Another caller left a blunt threat for a U.S. senator: “I’m going to murder you, and I’m going to start with your children.”

A state attorney general received this three-word missive: “Bang, bang, bang.”

Serving in public office in the United States is dangerous. From state and local government to Congress, an unending river of violent threats is washing through the mailboxes, offices, voice mail and texts of those who govern the nation. Thousands of public servants are living, working and, in the final weeks of election season, campaigning in a state of fear.

And it’s getting worse, officeholders said in dozens of interviews.

An investigation by The New York Times examining hundreds of records obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, court documents and law enforcement logs has found that, over a two-year period from 2024 to August of this year, thousands of violent threats inundated the lives of elected officials in unprecedented ways.

Some threats were vague; some were frighteningly specific. They promised torture, stabbing, rape and murder. They aimed at Republicans and Democrats alike, and at a range of officeholders from county clerks to United States senators. They targeted spouses, parents, siblings and children.

At least 44 governors, as well as their staff and families, have been subjected to violent threats over the past two years, The Times’s investigation found. That’s also true of at least 70 of the nation’s 100 senators, and at least 185 members of the House of Representatives — nearly half the body. More than half of the country’s secretaries of state, most of whom serve as their states’ chief election officers, have received threats of violence.

Actual violence also spiked during that period: assassination attempts against Donald Trump, the killing of Charlie Kirk, the assassination of a legislative leader and her husband in Minnesota, the firebombing of Gov. Josh Shapiro’s home in Pennsylvania. For many elected officials, the escalation is a grim testament to the toxicity of violent rhetoric and how it can shake the country’s democratic institutions.

The threats have also reshaped private lives. Dozens of officials have fortified their homes, installed cameras and hired private security guards, often at their own expense. They’ve changed their daily routines, moved their children to new schools, grocery-shopped only at certain times and places. They’ve scrubbed the internet to remove personal information about themselves and their loved ones.

Some of them have altered what they say in public and, in rare cases, how they govern. Some, including members of Congress, have quit. Both parties have struggled to recruit candidates, especially women.

And policing violent threats against officials is a difficult task. The Times’s review of federal court data from the past two years found only 53 cases in which individuals were charged with threatening public officials, excluding the president.

Vague state and federal laws and free speech protections can make prosecution challenging. Anonymous letters and screen names can be hard to track. The sheer volume of threats can make hunting down those responsible virtually impossible.

This new normal can also be measured in dollars spent. In the 2017-2018 election cycle, candidates for federal office spent roughly $6 million on security-related items, according to campaign finance records. In the current midterm cycle, candidates had already spent at least $25 million by Aug. 1, with the final general election sprint still to come. That excludes what many officials are spending from their own pockets.

Overall, the threats tallied by The Times are likely undercounts; state laws and communication policies bar many offices from disclosing security issues. Many members of Congress said privately that it’s hard to imagine any remaining offices on Capitol Hill that have not experienced a violent threat this decade.

The rhetoric is abetted by the anonymity of the internet, a polarized political landscape and the entrenched public opinion that politicians are not improving American lives. Those receiving threats include divisive figures who have juiced the increasingly belligerent tone of political rhetoric, as well as others who avoid inflammatory talk but are targeted for their policies, ideology or party affiliation.

Representative Derrick Van Orden, a Republican from Wisconsin seeking re-election next month, attended the “Stop the Steal” rally on Jan. 6, 2021, in support of President Trump’s false claim that he had won the 2020 election. Mr. Van Orden was outside the U.S. Capitol that day when a mob attacked it, though he has denied entering the building. He was elected to Congress in 2022.

That’s when the threats began.

“I was a Navy SEAL for over 22 years,” Mr. Van Orden said in an interview with The Times. “I hunted terrorists around the world a lot and was very successful at that. Never had a single threat to my family. Ever.”

Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

Representative Derrick Van Orden Republican, Wisconsin

Now, Mr. Van Orden travels with armed security personnel. His family, he said, is “protected 24 hours a day.”

For much of her political career, Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former Republican House member from Georgia, injected herself into the most pitched political battles. Her liberal foes said she courted controversy to raise her profile. But her rapid rise also came at a cost.

What started out as a flood of threats primarily from the left evolved into menace from the right, too, after Ms. Greene’s break with President Trump last fall.

Former Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene Republican, Georgia

Ms. Greene’s dispute with the president centered largely on Jeffrey Epstein, the sexual predator who eventually killed himself in jail. Like many on the far right, Ms. Greene had agitated for the release of government files pertaining to Mr. Epstein. Then she began agitating directly against the president she had once fawned over, when his government refused to do so.

Her disillusionment expanded after Mr. Trump took the country to war against Iran. She believed his tariff policies and curtailment of health subsidies were hurting her constituents in rural northwest Georgia, she said, and flouting his promise to put “America First.”

Her breaking point came after the president called her a “traitor.” Of the torrent of threats that followed, one stood out. It was aimed at her son.

“That’s the one that bothers me on a visceral level,” she said.

Ms. Greene reached out to Mr. Trump, hoping for compassion from a president she had stood by for years. She forwarded copies of the threats to him, hoping that seeing the threats against her family would be enough to tone down the attacks.

She got a five-word reply from the president: “Your fault, you deserve it.”

Weeks later, Ms. Greene announced her retirement from Congress.

“I looked at what are the risks and what is the reward,” she said. “And for me, it was, I’m not going to be treated that way, and I’m not going to have my children’s lives threatened.”

A White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, did not deny the contents of Mr. Trump’s text, but he said the president condemned political violence.

“Having survived multiple assassination attempts — and having seen his dear friend Charlie be assassinated last year — no one understands the dangers of political violence more than President Trump,” he said, referring to Mr. Kirk.

Women are often more aggressively targeted than men, and harder to recruit, said Greta Neubauer, the Democratic minority leader in the Wisconsin State Assembly. Mothers are more apt to avoid the risk to themselves and their families, she said.

If potential recruits don’t bring up fears of violence on their own, Ms. Neubauer does. “There is an amount of risk that you and your family are going to need to accept if you choose to do this,” she regularly says to potential candidates. “And we want to make sure that you are fully aware of that in advance.”

Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat from Minnesota, nearly walked away, too.

He was inundated with violent threats after Kamala Harris, then the vice president, selected him as her running mate in 2024. But it was the assassination of two close friends, the former Minnesota House speaker, Melissa Hortman, and her husband, Mark, in June 2025 that led Mr. Walz to question his resolve to keep going.

Gov. Tim Walz Democrat, Minnesota

The tragedy also altered Mr. Walz’s daily life. His security team was on increased alert. He felt helpless to protect state lawmakers who felt exposed and unsafe after losing one of their own.

“We’re a part-time legislature,” Mr. Walz said. “These folks go back home and teach school, run their business, they’re dentists, they’re nurses, they do all those things. How do you follow them in the nine months they’re not here?”

A former C.I.A. analyst and Defense Department official, Senator Elissa Slotkin had been trained to deal with a variety of “threat environments.”

Her family had not. So when political foes started targeting her parents, including an ailing father, Ms. Slotkin couldn’t shield them from a toll they had not invited.

Last November, Ms. Slotkin, a Democrat from Michigan, joined five others in a video telling U.S. soldiers that they did not have to follow unlawful orders.

The message infuriated Mr. Trump, who described it as “seditious behavior from traitors” and “punishable by death.” Conservatives labeled the lawmakers the “seditious six.” The threats poured in — especially to Ms. Slotkin, the one who had posted the video on the social-media platform X.

The Capitol Police assigned round-the-clock shifts to protect her. What they couldn’t prevent: her parents’ home being swatted in the middle of the night. Her father, 81 at the time, was dying of cancer when someone called the local police with a false report that a man was killing his wife at the couple’s address.

Senator Elissa Slotkin Democrat, Michigan

The senator’s brothers put security details in front of their homes. Staff members temporarily moved out of theirs. Her father died just a few weeks after the police came to his door.

“I signed up for this, but my family and my staff did not,” Ms. Slotkin said.

Threats to family and staff feel more chilling, several officials said, and the impacts are often more disruptive.

“My daughter just sent me one yesterday,” Mr. Walz told The Times, “where somebody said, ‘Wait what I’ve got in store for you — and then a picture in front of the house.”

Mr. Van Orden moved his family because of violent threats. “I know exactly what these people are trying to do,” he said. “To make me leave the public square through threatening my family, because they know threatening me has no effect at all because of my background.”

Many officials cite a desire to improve their country for their children and grandchildren as motivation for seeking office. The deluge of threats has done the reverse, pushing the civic-minded out of the public square to shield their loved ones from an increasingly toxic world.

Carly Koppes, a Republican county election official in Colorado, saw a new kind of violent threat after her pregnancy became public: messages targeting both her and her unborn child.

Carly Koppes Weld County, Colorado, clerk and recorderRepublican

Rodric Bray, the Republican leader of the Indiana Senate, drew critics, but rarely threats, after he became a well-known power broker in Indianapolis — until his chamber bucked Mr. Trump’s push to eliminate the state’s two remaining Democratic congressional districts.

Amid headline after headline about the intraparty disagreement, threats of violence overwhelmed the staid political atmosphere of the Indiana Statehouse. Mr. Bray became the main target.

Bomb threats were called into his office. Death threats, too. “They were very short,” he said. “Just saying, I’m going to come down there and kill you.” Same with messages about his house. “Just, ‘There’s going to be a bomb mailed to your house,’ or, ‘There’s been a bomb placed at your house.’”

Mr. Bray said he forced himself into a stressful state of high alert. He changed his daily routine. He talked with his family about staying “extra vigilant” around the house and away from home. Friends kept watch. Once, law enforcement noticed something suspicious on his patio, alarming neighbors and keeping family away until it was cleared.

Rodric Bray State senator, IndianaRepublican

Ms. Koppes said she, too, changed her hours and took different routes to work after learning that some threats against her had come from a man living directly across from her office. “Good day War Criminal,” one of them read. “You traitor guilty of treason and sedition; oath breaking piece of trash loser, you should get gang raped.”

Shenna Bellows, the Democratic secretary of state in Maine, and her husband moved out of their home after law enforcement told her it wasn’t safe to stay. Ms. Bellows, Maine’s chief election officer, had been receiving threats at least since 2020, when Mr. Trump and his allies persuaded thousands of his supporters, without evidence, that the election that year had been rigged.

Ms. Bellows was swatted in 2023, a day after she removed Mr. Trump from the state’s presidential primary ballot under the Constitution’s insurrection clause. She later reversed herself after a court ruled against a similar measure in Colorado, but the threats kept coming.

In January, someone posted her cellphone number and other personal information online. Menacing voice mail and text messages poured in. Her social media was inundated. “Shenna bellows I’m coming for you,” one person wrote, adding profanity. “beheaded soon.”

Shenna Bellows Secretary of state, MaineDemocrat

Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic member of the Texas House of Representatives, was out of state when an activist posted a picture of her home online. She urged her family to move in with relatives.

“It was a feeling of being hunted,” she said.

Now the Democratic candidate for governor in Texas, Ms. Hinojosa has installed new fencing and other barriers at home “so that we’re just not as easily accessible, we’re not as easily seen.”

Officials are also buying guns. Jennifer Johnson, a county judge in rural Florida, recently purchased one and enrolled in a firearms course after an animated video of her being murdered circulated online.

Security equipment has become a huge expenditure for officeholders. Much of it has come on Capitol Hill, where, in the wake of the Jan. 6 riot, threats of violence spiked dramatically.

J. Thomas Manger took over as chief of the Capitol Police in 2021. He more than doubled his roster of investigators. Offices were fortified and modernized. Furniture was scrutinized and rearranged. District offices across the country got security assessments.

The House’s sergeant-at-arms, who oversees security in that chamber and helps govern the Capitol Police, spent more than $28 million in 2025, the second most in recent history, according to congressional records.

J. Thomas Manger Former chief, Capitol Police

Among the expenditures: $1.8 million on an alert system, and more than $200,000 on a gunshot detection system.

By the time Mr. Manger retired in May 2025, the volume of threats had gotten worse, he said.

One reason is the difficulty of mounting prosecutions, which reduces the deterrent effect, he said. Fewer than 10 percent of the cases Mr. Manger’s team investigated in 2021 led to criminal charges, he said.

Some of that is due to mitigating circumstances such as a lack of a criminal record or mental health struggles. Some of it results from the use of diversion programs such as counseling.

Making a threat is also a tricky crime to prosecute. Explicit death threats against members of Congress are illegal, but some stop short of that line and are ruled menacing, not explicit.

“One member got a photograph, an actual physical photograph, mailed to them, and it was a photograph of their, I think it was an 8-year-old child walking a dog in their neighborhood,” Mr. Manger said. “All it said on it was ‘cute dog.’”

Some officeholders don’t control government purse strings. State lawmakers, election officials, council members and school board officials are often left to fend for themselves.

Ms. Hinojosa said that almost every fortification she’s undertaken has come at personal expense.

Threats have remade how candidates run for office. Outdoor events are increasingly rare. Sweeping event spaces is a regular part of campaign advance work. Metal detectors and frisks are common. Many candidates have a security official in their inner circle.

Such measures have made candidates feel isolated, yet the public has taken notice.

Gina Hinojosa State representative and candidate for governor, TexasDemocrat

For some, at a certain point, it all becomes too much.

Ms. Greene recalled that her feud with the president came shortly after the assassination of Mr. Kirk. That made the subsequent deluge of threats more personal and more frightening.

“I said, you know what? This is just not worth it for me personally,” she said. “I’m a very happy person without being in Congress. Much happier actually. And probably a lot safer.”

The Times filed more than 100 open records requests for this project, reviewing thousands of violent threats made in emails, handwritten notes, social media postings, voice mail messages and police reports. The Times conducted more than 30 interviews with current and former elected officials, law enforcement officials, election officials, security experts and political operatives, while reaching out individually to every member of Congress. The Times also used artificial intelligence to compile and filter thousands of pages of court documents. Each case was manually reviewed and confirmed by Times journalists.

Produced by Leo Dominguez, Jeffrey Furticella, Rebecca Halleck, Jacob Meschke and Rumsey Taylor.

item.title: After Many Threats, an Arizona Lawmaker Asks: ‘Is It Really Worth It?’
item.description:
Alma Hernandez’s home used to feel like her sanctuary. Now it feels like a fortress.

In recent years she has installed cameras, alarms and a lock that opens with her fingerprint. She put iron bars on her windows and a blinding floodlight on her front porch. She cut down two trees in her yard after the police told her they could aid an intruder, and her brother moved in to protect her when the death threats intensified.

Ms. Hernandez, an Arizona state representative since 2019, did not know she was signing up for a dangerous job. But these days, serving in public office increasingly means looking over your shoulder.

“Politicians are no longer treated like we’re human,” she said.

Ms. Hernandez, a fourth-term Democratic lawmaker who is Mexican American and Jewish, has received threats from the far left and the far right. They have come in response to her outspoken support for Israel, her championing of vaccines and her first campaign, which drew attention from David Duke, a former leader of the Ku Klux Klan.

Violent threats have arrived via her social media feed, her email inbox and her office phones. Her home address has been circulated online, and her mother has received menacing calls. Last year, an aide’s car parked outside Ms. Hernandez’s house was struck by gunfire. This year, state police opened an investigation after someone sent her a social media message pledging to “find, torture and brutally murder” her and her friends, along with one of her two Chihuahuas.

So pervasive are the threats that they have altered not only Ms. Hernandez’s life, but also those of her family, friends and neighbors, who now keep a close eye on her home and warn her about suspicious activity. The intimidation has even influenced her approach to policymaking.

“I’ve asked myself, ‘Is it really worth it?’” said Ms. Hernandez, 33, who was the youngest woman ever to be elected to the Arizona Legislature. “I do wonder now, why would any 25-year-old want to do this with their life?”

Across America, threats of violence haunt the daily existence of elected officials, their staff members and their families. A New York Times investigation has found that the nation’s highest-profile politicians — including governors and members of Congress — face consistent violent harassment.

Studies show that violent threats are also rising against lower-level elected leaders, who number more than 500,000 and serve in state legislatures, city councils and school boards.

In a survey conducted this year by Princeton University and CivicPulse, nearly 20 percent of 460 local elected officials across the country reported receiving threats during the first three months of 2026. Just like at the federal level, the perilous climate is pushing some local public servants out of office early and causing others to forgo running altogether, the researchers said.

But unlike national political figures, most state and local officials have few resources to help keep them safe. Faced with violent threats, they are often left to fend for themselves. And after a Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband were assassinated last year, many say they feel more exposed than ever.

City and town officials are even more vulnerable, experts say, and they have been targeted repeatedly in Arizona in recent years. The Bridging Divides Initiative, a research center based in Princeton’s policy school, found 57 confirmed threats against Arizona county and municipal lawmakers since 2022, a figure researchers say is an undercount.

In Maricopa County, home to Phoenix, death threats toward local officials surged after the 2020 election as President Trump’s unfounded claims of voter fraud fueled a torrent of conspiracy theories. One county supervisor was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and decided not to seek re-election, while threats to two other officials resulted in a prison sentence.

At the state level, legislators from both parties have been targeted. In 2022, a former middle school music teacher emailed Senator Wendy Rogers, a Republican, and vowed to shoot her in the head. Last year, Arizona’s secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, a Democrat, allowed candidates for office to use campaign cash to pay for security, citing the dangerous political environment.

That decision helped Analise Ortiz, a Democratic state senator. Last year, her online posts alerting residents that immigration agents were near a school attracted a string of sinister threats, including several that said she would be hanged.

“Walk around with security cause I promise you three months,” one person wrote. Another said Ms. Ortiz’s “car and home and family are easy to find.”

Ms. Ortiz made a list of safe places and lived in undisclosed locations for two weeks as the threats rolled in, she said.

“It’s remarkable that in the United States of America in 2026, as a state senator, I had to fear for my life,” said Ms. Ortiz, whose district is west of Phoenix.

When she returned home, Ms. Ortiz, one of the statehouse’s leading progressives, installed a camera system and petitioned a court to conceal her address.

She also bought a gun and trained to use it.

“It’s horrible we have to think that way,” Ms. Ortiz said. “But ultimately, my home and loved ones need to be protected.”

Ms. Ortiz and Ms. Hernandez represent opposing factions of Arizona’s Democratic Party, but they agree that violent rhetoric has reshaped both of their lives.

“What she experienced and what I experienced are symptoms of the same problem,” Ms. Ortiz said.

Political violence has long shadowed the Hernandez family, three members of which have held elected office. Ms. Hernandez’s brother, Daniel, was an intern for Representative Gabrielle Giffords in 2011 when the Democratic congresswoman was shot outside a Safeway in Tucson.

Mr. Hernandez, then 20 years old, provided first aid to Ms. Giffords as an ambulance raced to the scene. Mr. Hernandez, suddenly in the national spotlight, received his first death threat three days later.

“I’ve seen people at their most unhinged, or I thought I had,” said Mr. Hernandez, who went on to serve as a state representative. “And then it keeps getting worse.”

He said he had been shocked by the amount of hate — especially the antisemitism — directed at Ms. Hernandez and their sister, Consuelo Hernandez, another Democratic state lawmaker. By late 2023, he had become so worried that he insisted on moving into Alma Hernandez’s Tucson house for extra protection. He still lives with her part-time.

Ms. Hernandez first received threats during her first term, when one of her bills so angered vaccine opponents that they flooded her social media and office with ominous messages. The bill, which would have limited vaccine exemptions, went nowhere, but the furor transformed her work: Ms. Hernandez, who has a master’s degree in public health, now says she will never again sponsor pro-vaccine legislation. The cause isn’t worth the harassment, she said.

After Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, Ms. Hernandez said the number of threats increased. She said her vocal support for the Jewish state has drawn more violent messages in the last three years than any other time in her career.

Sam Segal, Ms. Hernandez’s boyfriend, has given her pepper spray and offered to teach her to use his firearms. They’ve also rehearsed chilling scenarios. If she’s attacked by a man, Mr. Segal has told her, “kick right in the middle and run.”

“You don’t know what’s legit and what’s not,” Mr. Segal said of the threats, many of which are anonymous. “There are extremists out there who will go the whole nine yards, and I can’t be with her 24/7.”

The threats have made the couple nervous about having children, they said.

“Would we be OK with bringing a family into this environment?” Ms. Hernandez said. “Quite frankly, the answer right now is no.”

A scary moment unfolded last year, just one day before Minnesota’s former House speaker was killed.

Mr. Hernandez, who was then running for Congress, was meeting with his campaign team at Ms. Hernandez’s house when a bullet shattered the window of his aide’s car, which was parked outside. The police never found the shooter, nor did they determine whether the gunfire was targeted. But the incident deeply rattled the family.

If Ms. Hernandez wins her election in November, she will serve a two-year term in the State Senate.

She said she had not thought much about her political future beyond that. But if she could go back in time, she said, she would choose a quieter, less stressful way to begin her career.

“I would tell Alma almost nine years ago, ‘Girl, wait. Go live your life,’” Ms. Hernandez said. “This has not been an easy time.”

Nick Corasaniti contributed reporting.

item.title: In the Senate, Collins Often Defies Trump but Rarely Stops Him
item.description:
It was approaching midnight on the Senate floor, and a vote that had been meant to last 15 minutes had dragged on for nearly three hours as Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, weighed whether to kill one of President Trump’s top priorities.

It was hardly the first time she had faced such a choice.

Throughout Mr. Trump’s two terms, Ms. Collins had frequently criticized the president and voted against his initiatives more often than anyone else in her party. She cherished her reputation as one of the few remaining independent-minded Republicans in the Senate, which helped explain her enduring popularity in her purple home state. Yet she had more rarely blocked the president’s agenda outright.

On that night last summer, Ms. Collins had the chance to do so. The senator, the chairwoman of the committee that controls federal spending, was deeply opposed to a bill Mr. Trump had demanded to cancel $9 billion in foreign aid and public broadcasting money that Congress had approved.

She had prepared an amendment to shield the Corporation for Public Broadcasting from the cuts, a move that had bipartisan support. But if she succeeded, conservatives loyal to the president would all but certainly refuse to back the spending cuts. Given Republicans’ slim majority, their opposition could have doomed the bill, blocking Mr. Trump’s plan altogether.

After hours of wavering, Ms. Collins decided not to try to make the change. In what amounted to a largely symbolic move, she voted “no,” on the bill, registering her opposition to revoking the spending even though it was clear the measure had enough Republican votes to pass.

That is just what happened. A week later, the cuts were enacted as Mr. Trump wanted.

As Ms. Collins runs for a sixth term this year in a race that has the potential to determine control of the Senate, the episode encapsulates the tension at the heart of her political identity. It has fueled one of the most dominant and long-running lines of attack against her: that she only defies the president when it doesn’t matter.

A New York Times analysis of Ms. Collins’s voting record over the last decade paints a more complicated picture. It shows that she breaks with her party more than any other Republican senator. It also reveals that her defections — which frequently helped Democrats block parts of Mr. Trump’s agenda during his first two years in office — have rarely thwarted the president during his second term.

Ms. Collins, the lone congressional Republican remaining in New England and the chairwoman of the powerful Appropriations Committee, has had her share of major ruptures with Mr. Trump, including when she cast a critical vote in 2017 against repealing the Affordable Care Act and when she voted in 2021 to convict him in his second impeachment trial. It is a record she often cites as proof of her independence from the president as she runs in a state that he lost three times.

The Times’s analysis found that during the current Congress, Ms. Collins has broken with her party 17 percent of the time on votes in which lawmakers mostly divided along partisan lines — more than any other Republican senator.

That is roughly in line with the frequency of her defections during the first Trump administration, though the number has grown as partisan votes have become much more common. But her success rate when she breaks with other Republicans — the times when her vote helps Democrats’ position prevail — has steeply declined.

These are all of the votes during the first and second Trump administrations in which the two parties diverged and Ms. Collins broke with Republicans.

During the first two years of Mr. Trump’s first term, Ms. Collins’s helped thwart his plans roughly half the time she opposed them. Those instances included stopping Mr. Trump’s attempts to repeal President Barack Obama’s health care law, opposing military assistance to Saudi Arabia and blocking an effort to rescind billions of dollars from the Children’s Health Insurance Program. When Ms. Collins has sided with Democrats over the past two years — such as when she opposed Mr. Trump’s spending cuts, his tariffs and, more recently, switched her vote on the war with Iran — her position has prevailed only 15 percent of the time.

Phoebe Keller, a spokeswoman, said that in a statement that Ms. Collins had long demonstrated a willingness to vote in the best interest of her constituents, regardless of which president was in power, and denied that she limited such breaks to instances where her party could afford to do without her vote.

“She has supported them when she agrees and does not hesitate to vote against the administration when she disagrees,” Ms. Keller said.

But her defections appear to have made less difference in recent years. To some extent, this reflects the increasingly polarized nature of the Senate, in which Ms. Collins has found fewer Republicans willing to join her in defying Mr. Trump. As the president has tightened his hold on the Republican Party, chasing moderates and establishment figures like her out of Congress, they have mostly been replaced by hard-right figures who seldom break ranks.

It also reflects how Senate leaders have adapted to contend with Ms. Collins’s views and the political challenges she faces at home. Top Republicans often factor Ms. Collins’s straying from the party line into their strategy on major bills, changing provisions for her or working to persuade enough other G.O.P. senators to stay in the fold to keep the agenda on track while allowing her to defect.

That was the case with Republicans’ signature domestic policy law — what Mr. Trump refers to as his “big, beautiful bill” — which slashed taxes, significantly increased funding for immigration enforcement and made substantial cuts to social safety net programs.

Ms. Collins voted against the bill, expressing deep reservations about its cuts to Medicaid. But she did not stand in the way of Republicans as they sought to bring it to the floor, siding with her party on a key procedural vote that cleared the way for its eventual passage.

Ms. Collins said that vote was necessary to start debate on the bill so she could seek to reverse or limit the health care cuts she opposed. And she noted that it allowed her the chance to add language securing a fund for rural health care providers meant to blunt the legislation’s effects in Maine.

But in the end, Ms. Collins could not kill or even limit the Medicaid cuts. And Republican leaders turned elsewhere to muster the votes they needed to pass the measure over her objections. They labored overnight to win support from Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, loading the bill with a raft of sweeteners including exempting her state from several of the new work requirements the legislation imposed on recipients of social safety net programs.

Republicans have also been forced to maneuver around Ms. Collins to secure confirmation for some of Mr. Trump’s cabinet nominees. She has for decades followed a longstanding Senate tradition of deferring to the president on such picks, including when Democrats controlled the chamber during President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s term. Over that period, she sided with Democrats more on more than half the votes that were split among partisan lines — a far higher rate of defection than when her own party had control — backing hundreds of Biden nominees, The Times’s analysis found.

Ms. Collins has argued that such votes have helped her work with presidential nominees on issues of concern to Maine, including recently on tariff exemptions. But in some cases, she has refused to back Mr. Trump’s selections, including Todd Blanche for attorney general and Pete Hegseth for secretary of defense.

Ms. Collins did not bring down either nominee. Mr. Hegseth was confirmed after Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who had been working to kill Mr. Hegseth’s nomination and had signaled to Ms. Collins and Ms. Murkowski that he would join them in opposition, had a sudden change of heart and cast the deciding vote in favor.

And after Mr. Blanche’s nomination advanced to the Senate floor, Ms. Collins was the first in a group of undecided senators to announce she would not support him. Mr. Blanche was confirmed after Senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican leaving office this year, apparently swallowed his objections.

Still, Democrats have criticized Ms. Collins for voting to confirm several of Mr. Trump’s other nominees only to later vocally condemn them or actions they have taken.

One such vote in particular has come back to haunt Ms. Collins, a supporter of abortion rights, in her current campaign: her decision in 2018 to cast a critical vote to confirm Brett M. Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court. Justice Kavanaugh would join the conservative majority that overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. Ms. Collins has said that he “misled” her about his position on Roe, but that she does not regret backing him.

More recently, she voted to confirm Russell T. Vought, the White House budget director, who at the time of his nomination had aggressively challenged Congress’s power to control federal spending, repeatedly arguing that the president could withhold money appropriated by Congress.

Ms. Collins said then that she believed presidents were entitled to “broad discretion when selecting cabinet secretaries” and was focused on “whether the person is qualified for the job.” Ms. Keller, her spokeswoman, said that Ms. Collins continued to work closely with Mr. Vought on spending bills.

But in the time since Mr. Vought’s confirmation, she has angrily objected to a litany of moves he has made to defy congressional intent on spending, including the $9 billion rescissions package she voted against; the move to permanently layoff furloughed workers during last year’s government shutdown; the White House’s rejection of funding for scientific research approved by lawmakers; and the freezing of $600 million Congress appropriated for an international partnership helping developing countries buy and distribute vaccines.

Last month, the White House notified Congress that it was pursuing its second effort to unilaterally cancel spending without the approval of lawmakers using a tactic known as a “pocket rescission.” Ms. Collins called it “a clear violation of the law.”

“This is the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget to undermine Congress’s constitutional power of the purse,” Ms. Collins said. “I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.”

About the data

For its analysis of senators breaking with their parties, The Times focused on votes in which the two major parties diverged. Specifically, The Times selected votes in which at least 60 percent of one party’s participating members voted “yea” and 60 percent of the other party’s participating members voted “nay.” The Times calculated how often, during such votes, each senator voted against his or her party’s majority. The analysis excluded votes in which at least half of a party’s members did not vote.

The Times used data from Voteview covering votes through mid-September 2026. The Times included all types of votes, not only those concerning the passage of bills.

Because the four independent senators active during the time period analyzed all caucused with Democrats, The Times counted their votes toward the Democratic Party totals.

item.title: Republicans Held Onto the Great Plains for Years. Now They’re Nervous.
item.description:
Across the Great Plains, a region that Republicans have dominated for a generation, Democratic and independent candidates are polling well and expanding the electoral battlefield.

States that seldom swing could determine control of Congress. Governorships are up for grabs. Commercial breaks during college football games have become montages of attack ads.

The close races have turned the region’s challenges, like soaring diesel costs and the struggling cattle industry, into top-tier national issues. Democrats, who have long struggled to connect with rural voters, are now focused on turning angst over President Trump’s policies into support for their candidates. And Republicans are pouring advertising money into Kansas and sending Mr. Trump to stump in Oklahoma and Nebraska, proof that voters have real races on their ballots.

“They’re in trouble,” said Judy Vohland, a former Democratic Party chair in the conservative Central Nebraska county where Mr. Trump spoke last week. Otherwise, she asked, “Why the hell would you come out to Grand Island, Nebraska?”

Whether Republicans’ new vulnerability translates into losses is highly uncertain. The party has decades’ worth of voter good will and political infrastructure in the region, and Democrats have a tarnished brand and limited resources.

Still, Democrats and independents see an opening.

When Lynne Walz, Nebraska’s Democratic nominee for governor, held an event last week in a county that Mr. Trump carried by nearly 50 percentage points in 2024, there were more attendees than chairs to seat them. She was introduced by a former Republican state senator from the area who said he could not recall ever voting for a Democrat, but that he planned to cast his ballot for Ms. Walz rather than Gov. Jim Pillen, the Republican incumbent.

“There’s a lot of Republicans out here taking a look,” said the former senator, John Stinner, who described Ms. Walz as someone who worked across party lines in the Legislature.

Competitive campaigns for governor and Senate have positioned Kansas and Nebraska as bona fide battlegrounds, while Texas and Plains-adjacent Iowa also have several close races. So unsettled is the landscape that even some contests in dark-red Oklahoma and South Dakota have entered the periphery of flippability.

National Democrats recently added the Oklahoma City-area seat held by Representative Stephanie Bice to their target list, and the party is even eyeing the governorship. In South Dakota, the independent candidate Brian Bengs has released polls showing him within striking distance of Senator Mike Rounds, the Republican incumbent.

The weaker party in Washington often has a strong midterm election, and Democrats made some inroads on the Plains at the midpoint of Mr. Trump’s first term. But the breadth of this year’s battleground is energizing the Democratic base, and revealing erosion in parts of Mr. Trump’s coalition that once appeared unshakable.

Ryan Horn, a Republican strategist from Nebraska, described a “double- or triple-whammy” of steel tariffs, energy prices and fertilizer costs that had hurt farmers, testing the strength of the Republican base on the Plains more than in other regions.

“Farmers and ranchers who have been very reliably Republican, I think there’s a number of them that are thinking, ‘I want to use my vote to try to get some change,’” Mr. Horn said.

In Dodge City, Kan., a deeply Republican area with a large meatpacking industry, Jaquan Graves said he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 thinking that he would boost the economy. Mr. Graves said he had repeatedly been disappointed by the president.

When Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers descended on his small city last month, alarming even some of the president’s most loyal allies in agriculture, Mr. Graves said he delivered meals to neighbors who were scared to venture outside.

“When ICE raided Southwest Kansas, right then and there, I knew that I had messed up,” said Mr. Graves, a political independent who ran unsuccessfully for City Commission last year. He said he would vote for Democrats this year for governor and Senate.

To flip votes in Republican territory, Democrats must overcome skepticism about their policies, especially on social issues. At Ms. Walz’s event outside Gering, in Nebraska’s Panhandle, Sylvia Coffey told the candidate that she wanted to “make sure that girls are in girls’ restrooms and lockers, and boys are in boys’ restrooms.”

In an interview, Ms. Coffey, a retired farmer and Republican who voted for Mr. Trump three times, said she also had concerns about the president’s rhetoric and low teacher pay. Although she still planned to vote for the Republican incumbent for Senate, she said she was leaning toward voting for Ms. Walz for governor.

“I think people are wanting changes,” she said.

Across the state in suburban Omaha, Michael Tiedeman, the chairman of the Sarpy County Republicans, said he was optimistic that Republicans would hold onto statewide offices, even as he acknowledged that some voters were frustrated during the second Trump administration.

“It takes time,” Mr. Tiedeman said. “Eighteen months is not enough time to enact an agenda and policy and start providing on campaign promises.”

Mr. Tiedeman’s county includes a portion of Nebraska’s politically mixed Second Congressional District, which Democrats are optimistic about flipping this year.

In Nebraska last week, Mr. Trump signed an executive order aimed at easing diesel costs, defended his decision to go to war in Iran and expressed confidence about the upcoming election.

“We’re going to beat them big,” Mr. Trump told the crowd in Grand Island, where he appeared alongside Mr. Pillen, the governor. “This is the most important midterm election.”

Recent history suggests that Mr. Trump’s confidence might be justified. Going straight north on the Plains from Oklahoma to North Dakota, Republicans hold all 10 U.S. Senate seats, four of five governorships and 13 of 14 U.S. House seats. (Two Kansans, Gov. Laura Kelly and Representative Sharice Davids, are the Democratic exceptions.)

Republicans also have an opportunity to expand their grip on the Plains this year, with Ms. Kelly barred by term limits from seeking re-election in Kansas. Recent nonpartisan polls have shown Kansas’ Republican nominee for governor, State Senator Ty Masterson, leading the Democratic candidate, State Senator Cindy Holscher, in a close race.

The Plains turned bright red only recently. For much of the 1990s, both of Nebraska’s senators were Democrats. In the 2000s, Oklahoma had a Democratic governor, and both of North Dakota’s senators were Democrats. The Democratic leader in the U.S. Senate, Tom Daschle, was from South Dakota.

But the nationalization of politics and Democrats’ positions on social, climate and agricultural issues torpedoed their competitiveness in statewide elections.

Republicans now routinely win 80 to 90 percent of the vote in some rural Plains counties, often offsetting Trump-era Democratic gains in suburbia.

“To a certain extent, and with good reason, Democrats were becoming perceived as more elitist,” said Mr. Daschle, the South Dakota Democrat who served as his party’s leader in the U.S. Senate before narrowly losing re-election in 2004.

Mr. Daschle said his party’s opportunity to start building back on the Plains this year was real but daunting.

“We’re not out of the woods when it comes to branding,” he said. “We have a big problem that way, and we have to redefine ourselves as Democrats.”

In many races this year, the choice of candidates reflects an awareness of that reality.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor hoping to become the state’s first Democrat in the Senate since the 1930s, has led or been even with Senator Roger Marshall in recent polls. In Nebraska and South Dakota, Democrats are not fielding a candidate for U.S. Senate, instead allowing independent candidates to challenge Republican incumbents.

And when Ms. Walz introduced herself to voters in Gering, she started by reminiscing about her childhood on a hog farm and talking about her Christian faith.

Asked in an interview about the Democratic brand and any issues where her views diverged from the party platform, Ms. Walz demurred.

“Honestly, I don’t pay attention to national party platforms,” Ms. Walz said. “I pay attention to what’s happening here in Nebraska. I really do. And I think that makes me not a party person.”

item.title: How the White House Manufactured a Narrative About a Trump Aide’s Call Logs
item.description:
On the afternoon of Friday, Oct. 2, the White House invited a mix of mainstream and right-wing reporters to an online briefing about “weaponization.” A briefer previewed records the White House planned to release from the investigation of Donald J. Trump’s retention of classified documents while out of office, and his obstruction of their retrieval.

The files reflected scattered topics. Among them: an internal debate over probable cause to search Mr. Trump’s social club and residence, Mar-a-Lago; plans to execute any search warrant while Mr. Trump and his family were away; and the collection of phone logs of Mr. Trump’s top aide, Susie Wiles.

Most facts were already known or minutiae, and mainstream reporters ignored the files when the White House posted them on Monday. But Trump allies pushed an alarmist and decontextualized interpretation through the conservative information ecosystem. By Wednesday, a reporter from Trump ally and MyPillow founder Mike Lindell’s website asked Mr. Trump about it in the Oval Office. The president thanked her for the question, denouncing the inquiry as “weaponization.”

“They did things to people that were associated with us that nobody should have been able to do, and it all came out just recently in the files,” Mr. Trump said.

The episode shows how the Trump administration and its allies selectively disclose government files, omitting context to discredit investigations that led to Mr. Trump’s federal indictment and that anger his supporters. As the midterm elections approach, it also shows how a grievance narrative can be manufactured and inserted into national political discourse.

The Oct. 2 briefing was led by John Solomon, a former mainstream journalist who is now employed by the White House as a so-called special government employee. He has been active for years in presenting pro-Trump narratives, including during the 2019 events related to Ukraine that led to Mr. Trump’s first impeachment. In 2022, Mr. Trump named him his representative to the National Archives so he could gain access to records related to the investigation into the 2016 Trump campaign’s ties to Russia.

Mr. Solomon chairs a White House “transparency” task force that has released batches of government documents on more than half a dozen occasions since July. The documents appear to have been selected to bolster narratives Mr. Trump has promoted, including those that cast doubt on the integrity of U.S. elections and seek to discredit investigations into his conduct.

In an interview, Mr. Solomon acknowledged conducting the briefings. He said that he is unpaid and has no security clearance, but that about half-dozen task force officials do. He said he suggests categories to search, and task force officials sift through “millions of pages” for responsive documents. The White House counsel then declassifies them.

Mr. Solomon said he is briefed in advance on the files’ contents, but sees them only shortly before briefing other journalists. He described himself as a “pool reporter” — the term for a reporter chosen to share information with a larger group of news organizations when there is not enough room for all to fit — seeking more information for the public. He said he always encourages journalists to do their own reporting.

“It isn’t an effort at subterfuge,” he said. “It isn’t an effort at not giving you something in context. It’s giving you what the government made available and then giving you a chance to go find the rest of the story.”

Mainstream reporters have only occasionally found news in Mr. Solomon’s presentations. But once he completes his role as White House briefer, he writes articles based on the same material for his website, JustTheNews.com. In this case, his article — like his briefing — presented known information as revelations and omitted key context about new details. Its narrative entered a right-wing media echo chamber.

Mr. Solomon highlighted a paragraph from an F.B.I. Washington field office email from July 2022 saying that the office, unlike Justice Department counterespionage prosecutors, “does not believe” the available evidence established probable cause that Mr. Trump was still illegally keeping more classified documents at Mar-a-Lago. At issue was whether there was sufficient evidence to justify a search warrant.

On a podcast the following Monday with the right-wing commentator Benny Johnson, Mr. Solomon said the first of “three major revelations in the documents” was that before the Mar-a-Lago raid, “very senior F.B.I. officials, including an assistant director, raised concerns that the F.B.I. had not met the probable cause standard for authorizing a raid,” but “were overruled.”

That paragraph was not a revelation. It has been public since last December, when the F.B.I. gave Senator Charles E. Grassley, Republican of Iowa, files containing it verbatim. Mr. Grassley and conservative news outlets had highlighted it then just as Mr. Solomon did in his briefing and Monday reporting.

Mr. Solomon’s presentation, both times, also omitted key context: The field office’s legal doubts came before Mar-a-Lago surveillance footage emerged that showed a Trump aide moving boxes from a storage area before a lawyer came to search it for subpoenaed classified files. The additional evidence resolved legal concerns about probable cause.

The Washington field office’s assistant director, Steven D’Antuono, has testified that he and his team continued to urge officials to try again to obtain Mr. Trump’s voluntary compliance with the subpoena before escalating to a search — but for prudential, not legal, reasons. (The eventual search recovered more than 100 classified documents that Mr. Trump had not turned over when purporting to comply with the subpoena.)

A more complicated example involves Ms. Wiles’s phone logs. She ran Mr. Trump’s political action committee while he was out of office, then his 2024 campaign. She is now the White House chief of staff.

The files showed that in early to mid-2023, investigators — operating under Jack Smith, the special counsel appointed to oversee the federal inquiries into Mr. Trump — logged Ms. Wiles’s calls using a device known as a pen register, which creates a record of who called whom and when, but does not collect conversation content. The F.B.I. can get a court order to use one if a judge agrees that a low legal standard — mere “relevance” to an investigation — is met.

The collection of her call logs was already known. Court filings in 2024 showed that her phone records since January 2021 had been subpoenaed from a phone company. (The material identified her as “Person 49,” but accompanying excerpts from her April 7, 2023, investigative interview pointed to her identity.) Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director, told Reuters in February that the agency had subpoenaed Ms. Wiles’s phone logs in 2022 and 2023.

The actual news, then, was subtle: Investigators had used a pen register in addition to subpoenas, meaning they had logged her calls in real time in addition to collecting logs of her past calls. By omitting that context, right-wing news accounts created the sensational impression that the scrutiny of her call activity itself was a revelation.

The White House did not release case-file material explaining why officials and a judge might have deemed Ms. Wiles’s call logs relevant to the investigation, leaving that to imagination or insinuation. But two reasons for investigators’ interest in her are known.

She was a witness. According to the indictment, Mr. Trump showed her a classified map, evidence he knew he possessed such records. More broadly, she oversaw his political action committee’s hiring and payment of lawyers provided to his employees who were also witnesses.

Investigators suspected that this could have been a scheme to monitor and shape testimony by the employee-witnesses about Mr. Trump, although they did not find sufficient evidence to charge any such conspiracy.

The indictment, for example, said a decision to pay for the defense of a Mar-a-Lago property manager — eventually Mr. Trump’s co-defendant, charged with conspiring to cover up the box movements — followed confirmation in a Signal chat with Ms. Wiles that the worker remained “loyal” to Mr. Trump and would do nothing to affect their relationship.

The “Person 49” material released in 2024 included Ms. Wiles’s call logs with Stanley Woodward Jr., now a senior Justice Department official. Mr. Trump’s political action committee hired him to represent both the Trump aide who moved the boxes — who also became a co-defendant — and a computer worker at Mar-a-Lago.

But the computer worker later replaced Mr. Woodward with his own lawyer, then told investigators for the first time that Mr. Trump, via the property manager, had pushed him to delete surveillance footage of the box movements, according to the indictment.

The court files released in 2024 also show that in her April 7, 2023, interview, a prosecutor pressed Ms. Wiles on whether free lawyers were contingent on employees not divulging damaging things about Mr. Trump. She “unequivocally” denied it.

The newly released material included F.B.I. reports flagging Ms. Wiles’s “contacts of interests”: about 20 lawyers, half a dozen journalists, political advisers and Mr. Trump. There were bursts of such calls around key moments, like her April 7 interview.

The names of lawyers are redacted. Mr. Solomon described investigators as having “tracked Trump defense lawyers’ calls.” That framing is misleading; they were tracking Ms. Wiles’s calls, not logging the lawyers’ calls with other people. It is not clear from the files, moreover, who each lawyer’s client was. Some might have been representing employee-witnesses.

Ms. Wiles’s six reporter contacts included Mr. Solomon, who left his name unredacted; names of reporters at ABC News, CNN, The New York Times, Politico and The Washington Post were blacked out. In promoting the files, Mr. Solomon expressed incredulity at how that could be of legitimate interest to investigators.

The missing context: As news reports recounted nonpublic investigative developments like grand jury subpoenas and sealed court rulings, Mr. Trump, his campaign spokesman and sympathetic commentators kept blaming Mr. Smith’s team for the leaks, accusing them of prosecutorial misconduct. (Unlike prosecutors, subpoena recipients may discuss grand jury matters.)

After publishing his account Monday morning, Mr. Solomon appeared on right-wing podcasts, including Stephen K. Bannon’s and Mr. Johnson’s, repeating his decontextualized account and suggesting the activity was unconstitutional.

By afternoon, other right-wing outlets emphasized another released file. It showed that when searching Mar-a-Lago was first proposed in May 2022, an F.B.I. official’s to-do list included determining travel plans for Mr. Trump, his wife Melania and their 16-year-old son Barron, all of whom lived there part of the year.

In context, officials wanted to do any search while the entire family was away, to keep it low key. Out of context, this was presented in sinister terms as the F.B.I. “tracking” Melania and a child. Around 4 p.m., for example, a Newsmax host opened an interview by asking the defense lawyer Alan Dershowitz if he objected to Mr. Smith and the F.B.I. having “tracked” Melania and Barron Trump. He called it “terrible.”

Late that afternoon, the National News Desk of Sinclair, a conservative owner of many local stations, distributed a similar segment for the evening newscasts of its stations. Fox News posted a similar article, but included the context for checking the Trumps’ travel plans.

The New York Post went further, inaccurately reporting: “Biden F.B.I. tracked Melania and Barron Trump’s travel — and even tapped Susie Wiles phone, documents show.”

The tapping claim was unambiguously false. The documents did not describe wiretapping, which means eavesdropping on private conversations. The legal difference is significant: Fourth Amendment privacy rights cover call content but not call logs, the Supreme Court has said.

Mr. Trump’s top policy aide, Stephen Miller, shared the New York Post headline and declared, “This was a seditious conspiracy against the Republic waged from within the Department of Justice and at the highest levels of government.” Representative Randy Fine, Republican of Florida, reposted it, too, declaring, “This is 1000 times worse than Watergate.”

That Tuesday evening, Mr. Trump’s social media account fanned the narrative, posting another right-wing site’s story: “Jack Smith Spied on Trump Staffer’s Communications and 20+ Lawyers: Report.” Then came Wednesday’s Oval Office question from Mr. Lindell’s reporter.

On Thursday morning, Fox News ran another article covering essentially the same ground as Monday’s.

And on Friday, the White House press office again invited selected reporters to another late afternoon briefing on “weaponization.” Another document release was coming.

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: In Unlikely Turn, Law and Order Heats Up L.A. Mayor’s Race
item.description:
Like most big cities, Los Angeles has steep challenges: homelessness. Extreme weather. Housing affordability. Budget shortfalls. Law and order has for years been a relative bright spot. Not since the 1960s has the city experienced such a low homicide rate.

In an unlikely turn, however, public safety has emerged as an abrupt flashpoint in the city’s fierce mayoral contest. Last Tuesday, Nithya Raman, the challenger, vowed to replace the police chief if elected. Two days later, Mayor Karen Bass stood next to the chief as they applauded a sweeping crackdown on drug dealing on Skid Row.

Points of contention between the two Democrats have included 911 wait times, who would best handle security for the 2028 Olympics and who did or did not use the words “fascist liar” to describe the police chief.

The traditional Republican argument that Democrats are soft on crime has been losing steam this election cycle as crime rates drop across the country. G.O.P. candidates are neverthelessi making a go of it in places like Michigan, where they are going after Abdul El-Sayed in the Senate race, and North Carolina, where Roy Cooper has been under attack in another Senate contest.

In liberal Los Angeles, though, politics are more blue-on-blue, and the usual dividing lines on law and order have been scrambled this year as a Democrat and a democratic socialist take different tacks on the police force as they vie for the city’s top elected post.

In a year of resounding success for democratic socialists around the country, the election in the nation’s second-largest city is also poised to test whether that organization has shed its image of demonizing the police that lingers from the days of protests over George Floyd’s death.

Ms. Raman, 45, is a Harvard-educated policy expert backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, an organization that has argued that law enforcement receives too large a share of public funding. Ms. Bass, 73, has made her career as a progressive leader, but has been criticized for being too aligned with the police, whose union has endorsed her and spent significantly to back her re-election.

And as the two women, formerly allies, enter the homestretch, the city’s conventional political wisdom has been upended by a Trump-like Republican influencer who in June placed third in the mayoral primary, failing to make the runoff.

That influencer, Spencer Pratt, whose house burned in the Palisades fire, railed at City Hall and charged that Democrats had let the city degenerate into a wasteland of identity politics and homeless “zombies.” Brash and far-reaching, Mr. Pratt’s argument was also heavy on law and order, and he repeatedly pointed to the squalid streets of Skid Row in downtown Los Angeles as evidence that the city was being failed by liberals like Ms. Bass and Ms. Raman.

As they compete for his supporters, at stake is the 25.53 percent of the primary vote he won, a potentially pivotal bloc in a contest in which polls show roughly one voter in three is undecided.

“Spencer Pratt was a conservative outsider — he was tough on crime, and he wanted to shake up the system,” said Dan Schnur, a former Republican political consultant who now teaches political communications at several universities in California. And as polls show Ms. Raman starting to pull ahead, Mr. Schnur said, the two remaining candidates are each now vying for “exactly one half of Pratt’s persona.”

So Ms. Bass is now highlighting her record on crime as proof that she’s more centrist than Ms. Raman, Mr. Schnur said. And Ms. Raman, a relative unknown despite six years on the City Council, is seeking to show “that she’s more of an outsider than Bass.”

Those dynamics were on display last week as Ms. Raman’s campaign ramped up its social media to capitalize on her momentum, while Ms. Bass stood side by side with the Los Angeles police chief, Jim McDonnell, whom Ms. Raman has criticized for the department’s response last year during raucous immigration protests.

First Ms. Raman was filmed with a progressive online provocateur, Ed Choi, who asserted in the video that Los Angeles had become “extremely fascist” since Ms. Bass appointed Mr. McDonnell to lead the Police Department. Ms. Raman, who in 2024 had voted for Mr. McDonnell’s appointment, said the chief had not “met this moment,” noting the use of tear gas last year in quelling protests. Then she repeated a vow that if she is elected, she would hire “new leadership within the department.”

At the influencer’s behest, according to Ms. Raman’s campaign, she then joined him in reciting his tagline: “Only you can stop fascist liars!” As they spoke, an image of Ms. Bass appeared onscreen.

The video, which was posted by Ms. Raman’s campaign and then disavowed by her and removed when it drew backlash, was swiftly condemned by the mayor.

Ms. Bass charged that Ms. Raman did not “hold our police officers in high regard” and was “crossing the line” in “labeling them fascists.”

“It’s dangerous and extreme rhetoric, and it has no place in this city — let alone from someone trying to become mayor,” Ms. Bass said.

Ms. Raman’s campaign said she had been referring to federal immigration agents.Ms. Bass retorted that her challenger was “not ready for prime time.”

To suggest a search for a new police chief with the 2028 Olympics looming was “naïve,” Ms. Bass repeated in interviews and appearances with donors.

In an ironic twist, the Trump administration’s top prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli — who is often at odds with city Democrats over arrests and detention of immigrants — praised Ms. Bass for her “leadership” in supporting a sweep of about two dozen suspected midlevel drug peddlers. He warned against Ms. Raman’s D.S.A. supporters, some of whom advocate defunding or disarming the police.

Ms. Raman’s campaign points out that she has not called for the police to be disarmed or defunded. Rather, she wants civilian mental health and homelessness professionals to handle more calls that do not require an armed response. But Mr. Schnur noted that in Los Angeles, the debate among voters is less about ideology or policy than livability.

“When Los Angeles voters think about crime, they tend to do so not in the context of danger but rather disorder,” he said. “Crime and homelessness and even traffic and potholes add to the impression of whether a city is working or not.”

In a statement, Ms. Raman’s campaign pointed out that “911 wait times have gone up under Mayor Bass” and that “we have 1,500 fewer officers than we did several years ago, even though we’re paying half a billion dollars more each year.”

“That,” she added, “is a failure of public safety management.”

In an interview, the mayor, whose approval ratings dropped precipitously last year after it emerged that she had been out of the country when the Palisades fire erupted, did not deny that she hoped voters would look at the tens of thousands of homeless people who have been moved indoors on her watch and the historic lows in the city’s crime rates. She asserted that safety and livability have been enhanced in Los Angeles since 2022, when she was elected amid the pandemic wreckage.

“I’m certainly hoping that they’ll look at both of us,” she said, referring to voters, and added, “And then say, is this what I really want?”

item.title: Democrats Press Pentagon on Iran Civilian Deaths
item.description:
Democratic lawmakers are pressing the Pentagon to answer questions about U.S. airstrikes that killed civilians in Iran, in a possible preview of the party’s oversight agenda should it win control in the midterm elections next month.

The members focused on a strike in September in which three adults and two children at a wedding were killed. The strike also injured some 70 people.

In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the House Democrats have demanded the Pentagon provide an account of the strike on Sept. 1 as well as other incidents in which large numbers of civilians were killed.

“This is the latest in an alarming pattern of civilian casualty incidents in strikes carried out by the United States in Iran since the war began,” the lawmakers wrote.

The House Democrats, for now, have little leverage to pressure the Department of Defense for answers. But should the party take control one or both chambers of Congress, the issue of civilian casualties in the Iran war could well become a focus.

The effort, led by Representatives Jason Crow of Colorado, Sara Jacobs of California and Yassamin Ansari of Arizona, had 74 signatures in all, demonstrating broad concern within the Democratic caucus.

The Pentagon has not acknowledged responsibility for the strike, saying only that an internal review is underway by U.S. Central Command. But a visual investigation by The New York Times found that the wedding, in Kuhestak, Iran, was struck by a bomb that had been released by American forces as they carried out intense attacks in southern Iran.

Neither the Pentagon nor Central Command, the department within the military with responsibility over the Middle East, has provided granular details of its military operations in Iran or of potential errant strikes that killed civilians. The department has also closed the area of the Pentagon where the press used to work from and placed tight controls on reporters’ entering the building.

In addition to the strike on the wedding, there have been a number of incidents of civilian casualties, most notably an attack on a Navy base in southern Iran in the opening hours of the war that destroyed an elementary school, killing at least 175 people.

The members of Congress said the number of strikes that had killed civilians was troubling, as was the lack of transparency from the Trump administration over the war more broadly.

“We are deeply alarmed by the continued pattern of civilian casualties resulting from U.S. operations in the war in Iran, and the apparent lack of action and accountability from the Department,” the lawmakers wrote in the letter. “Acknowledging such incidents, accepting responsibility, and learning from them makes our forces stronger, more effective, and an example to the world. When we fail to do so, it has the exact opposite effect.”

The letter from the lawmakers cited both the reporting from The Times and The Washington Post.

In the letter, the lawmakers ask the Pentagon if the U.S. military carried out the strike and what the intended target was. They also ask for details about any investigation into the strike in Kuhestak.

The lawmakers have also reinstated their earlier demand for information about the Pentagon’s review of the strike on the elementary school. More broadly, they are seeking information about another strike in Lamerd, Iran, on that same day, Feb. 28, that also reportedly caused civilian deaths as well as an accounting of other possible errant strikes.

The letter to Mr. Hegseth was sent on Oct. 8 and released publicly Sunday.

Asked for comment, a Defense Department spokeswoman reiterated an earlier statement from Central Command that the reports of the strike on the wedding originated on Iranian state media. “The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the I.R.G.C.,” the statement said, referring to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

Mr. Crow, who helped lead the effort, is a former Army Ranger who served in the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Since joining Congress, he has consistently worked on the issue of harm to civilians in war. He was a driving force behind a law establishing the military’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence and other measures aimed at minimizing errant attacks on civilians.

He has also collaborated with Ms. Jacobs on the issue of civilian casualties. In 2022, the two lawmakers were part of a group that founded a caucus in Congress to help protect civilians during conflict.

But Mr. Crow has been in the cross hairs of Mr. Hegseth’s Pentagon. He was one of six lawmakers who recorded a video telling U.S. service members they did not need to obey unlawful orders. President Trump accused the lawmakers of sedition and treason.
